bib.title: A Technical Taxonomy of LLM Agent Communication Protocols

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "A Technical Taxonomy of LLM Agent Communication Protocols", Linus Sander, Habtom Kahsay Gidey, Alexander Lenz, Alois Knoll (Technische Universität München). arXiv 2606.19135v1 [cs.MA], 17 Jun 2026. Preprint, no venue stated.

COVERAGE: Text extraction worked and was clean. The text is 88,457 chars. I read pp. 1-24 in full (body, tables, conclusion), which is about 66,000 chars. I skimmed the reference list (pp. 24+) only for origins. There are no appendices, and I found no embedded instructions. The figures (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3) came through as text. I did not run the figure script.

VERDICT ON THE PAPER: It is a qualitative taxonomy with no experiments, no benchmarks and no measured numbers. The "numbers" are counts of 9 hand-classified protocols. It is on topic for protocols and agent communication (MCP, A2A), but only tangentially on topic for context engineering. It is useful for a short comparison table and a vocabulary, not as evidence. Several of its headline claims are speculation, and a few are inconsistent with its own tables (see PROBLEMS).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: The taxonomy has five dimensions (counterparty, payload, interaction state, discovery mechanism, schema flexibility), built by the Nickerson method in 5 iterations (3 empirical-to-conceptual, 2 conceptual-to-empirical) over 9 protocols.
  number: 5 dimensions, 5 iterations, 9 protocols
  setup: sample is open-source, actively maintained, with a runnable implementation. Agent Protocol was excluded for no commit since Jun 2024 and AITP for 20 GitHub stars (both accessed 7 Jul 2025). Sampled: MCP, A2A, LAP, agents.json, Agora, ANP, LMOS, ACP, agntcy.
  quote: "we conducted five iterations: the first three followed the empirical-to-conceptual approach, and the final two followed the conceptual-to-empirical approach."
  where: p.13 (Fig. 2 on p.14; selection criteria p.10)
- Claim: All agent-to-agent protocols in the sample have session state and hybrid payloads.
  number: 7 of 9
  setup: classification by the authors from public specs and docs. It is not tested empirically.
  quote: "If a protocol implements agent-to-agent communication (7 of 9), a session state functionality is always available."
  where: p.21
- Claim: Schema flexibility is trending up. Most protocols allow multiple predefined schemas, and two negotiate schemas at runtime (Agora, ANP).
  number: 7 of 9 allow multiple schemas, 2 of 9 evolving
  setup: same hand classification. Table 1 shows single=2, multiple=5, evolving=2, so "7 of 9" counts the evolving ones too.
  quote: "The majority of protocols permit multiple schema definitions (7 of 9), and two (2 of 9) additionally allow schemas to evolve during runtime."
  where: p.21
- Claim: MCP is classed as context-counterparty, stateless, static discovery, structured payload, multiple schemas. Even though agents discover server capabilities at runtime, discovery is static because the base address must be known in advance.
  number: none
  setup: core MCP as specified in refs [116, 117]. The paper does not discuss later MCP additions.
  quote: "although agents can discover a server's capabilities at runtime, the discovery mechanism dimension classifies MCP as static, since the requesting agent must still know the server's base address a priori"
  where: p.20 (Table 2, p.19)
- Claim: A2A is agent-counterparty, session state (tasks), centralized discovery via a registry option, hybrid payload, multiple schemas. It supports three discovery strategies, all using a JSON Agent Card: a well-known path on the agent's own domain, private sharing, or a registry. A2A positions itself as complementary to MCP.
  number: 3 discovery strategies
  setup: A2A spec per refs [118-121, 144]
  quote: "A2A, by contrast, supports three discovery strategies, all relying on a JSON Agent Card as the agent's self-description."
  where: p.20; Table 2 p.19; background p.10-11
- Claim: Discovery is mostly static or centralized.
  number: 4 centralized, 4 static, 1 hybrid
  setup: Table 1. Centralized = A2A, ANP, ACP, agntcy. Static = MCP, LAP, agents.json, Agora. Hybrid = LMOS. No protocol is marked decentralized or partially centralized in Table 1.
  quote: "Most protocols instead rely on either a centralized registry (4 of 9) or static configuration (4 of 9)."
  where: p.21
- Claim: Forecast, not a finding. There is short-term pressure to unify agent-to-agent and agent-to-context protocols, but long-term a federated, layered stack is likely, like OSI. The candidate layers are L1 identity and transport, L2 discovery (agents.json, LMOS), L3 execution (MCP), L4 interaction (A2A, LAP, ACP, agntcy), L5 deliberation (Agora, ANP).
  number: none
  setup: an argument from networking precedent. No data.
  quote: "The layering is a proposed instantiation of the federated-stack argument in Section 6.1, not an observed fact."
  where: Fig. 3 caption p.22; text p.21
- Claim: Applying Marro et al.'s communication trilemma (versatility, efficiency, portability, which cannot all be maximised), MCP-style rigid, stateless, structured protocols maximise efficiency and portability. Evolving-schema protocols (Agora, ANP) maximise versatility at the cost of token overhead and latency. A2A, LMOS and ACP sit in the middle.
  number: none (the overhead is asserted, not measured)
  setup: conceptual mapping only
  quote: "this adaptability introduces significant token overhead and latency during schema negotiation, severely reducing efficiency."
  where: p.22-23
- Claim: No surveyed protocol has privacy safeguards, compliance checks or policy enforcement.
  number: none
  setup: the authors' reading of the 9 specs. Security was not a dimension.
  quote: "A notable gap across all investigated protocols is the widespread absence of privacy safeguards, compliance checks, and policy enforcement mechanisms."
  where: p.21
- Claim: Short protocol descriptions useful for a notes table. LAP has /runs, /threads and /store (long-term memory). ACP is RESTful, from BeeAI/IBM under Linux Foundation governance, with registering ACP servers. ANP has three layers (identity, meta-protocol, application). Agora uses Protocol Documents negotiated at runtime. agents.json is built on OpenAPI.
  number: none
  setup: summaries of the protocols' own docs
  quote: "The main endpoints are /runs for executing agents, /threads for managing multi-turn conversations, and /store for long-term memory storage."
  where: p.11
- Claim: Three dimensions were rejected: initiative flow, simplicity, and persistent state. Persistent state was rejected because the protocol does not determine what nodes store. This matters for memory notes, since protocols carry only session state.
  number: none
  setup: authors' judgement
  quote: "the protocol itself does not determine what connected nodes ultimately store persistently."
  where: p.17

LIMITS
- The authors concede the taxonomy lacks dimensions for authentication and security, technical protocol detail, and policy and norms (p.23). They say classifying newly emerging protocols is future work.
- The sample is 9 protocols, selected by GitHub stars and activity as of 7 Jul 2025. It is a snapshot and has dated: the paper is dated June 2026 but classifies protocols as of mid-2025 specs.
- Classification is by the authors' reading, with no inter-rater check and no empirical test of any protocol. There are no latency, token or accuracy measurements.
- The paper never discusses context windows, token budgeting, tool-description cost or context management. The only mention is a background line on finite context windows (p.5). It is off-topic for context engineering proper, apart from MCP, stateless versus session state, and LAP /store.
- It says "Anthropic has not officially endorsed" A2A or agntcy as MCP extensions (p.21). This claim has probably dated.
- Whether the field ends up with one standard or several is left "an open question" (p.24).

BUILDS ON
- Nickerson et al. [104] for the taxonomy method.
- Marro et al. [26] (Agora; Agent Communication Trilemma).
- Yang et al. [103] (2-dimension taxonomy, 14 protocols; the counterparty dimension extends their object-orientation).
- Ahmed and Boutaba [141] (discovery values).
- Ling et al. [140] (state kinds).
- Eberendu [139] (data types).
- Related surveys: Li et al. [27], Du [101], Kong et al. [24], Ehtesham et al. [25] (compares MCP, ACP, A2A, ANP).
- Older protocols: KQML [99], FIPA ACL [100], Contract Net [109].
- Cerf and Kahn [97].

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig. 2 (p.14): the five dimensions and their values.
- Table 1 (p.18): classification matrix of the 9 protocols. This is the quickest comparison.
- Table 2 (p.19): per-protocol rationale, the best source for an MCP versus A2A comparison row.
- Fig. 3 (p.22): proposed five-layer protocol stack. The caption says it is proposed, not observed.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Internal inconsistencies:
  - The text (p.21) says only LMOS "truly incorporates a decentralized, peer-to-peer approach", yet Table 1 puts LMOS as hybrid and marks no protocol decentralized.
  - Table 2 describes Agora as "Decentralized" in its rationale but lists its discovery as Static.
  - ANP is described as peer-to-peer and decentralized (p.11) but classified Centralized.
  - The abstract says "decentralized discovery remains rare", which the tables do not support (zero in the table).
  - Fig. 3 puts MCP alone at L3 while calling the stack "not an observed fact".
- Cite this paper only for the taxonomy and the table, not for the forecast.
- Extraction path: /tmp/sander.txt (a scratch copy I made; not a deliverable).
